Section 4.3 discusses the infrastructure and operational implications beyond fuel cost for non drop-in fuels. 4.1 FUEL COST ANALYSIS OF LOCOMOTIVE ENERGY SYSTEMS USING BIOFUELS While some biofuel options (e.g., RD) can use existing infrastructure with no major modifications to locomotive engines, some emerging biofuel options (e.g., methanol, ammonia) may require additional engine modification and/or infrastructure support. In our preliminary analysis, we focused on the fuel cost of each biofuel. We assume the biofuels are either blended with RD directly or used in a dual-fuel configuration with a specific mix ratio. For each biofuel option, the mix ratio was selected based on the review of existing literature. Some biofuels (for example, methanol and ethanol) can be combined with diesel in multiple possible ways. These variations are based on engine configuration, fuel injection type, and use of additional admixtures and/or emulsifiers to mix two fuels together. In our study, we used the highest possible mix ratio for each option to maximize the biofuel use. We also investigated BD blends (BD20+ RD80), because this is a current way to use biofuel in railroad operations. For each biofuel mix, we estimated the fuel price of the mix based on the MFSP presented in Section 2.2. For the biofuels with multiple pathways, we considered the pathway with the lowest MFSP. The price for baseline conventional diesel was collected from DOE regional estimates from which we extracted the U.S. average diesel price for 2020.
